The Black madtom (Noturus funebris) is a small ictalurid catfish inhabiting streams and rivers of the southeastern United States. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum total length of 15 cm [Li = 15 cm], placing it among the smaller-bodied members of its genus. This ultimate size is reached only by particularly old individuals, as growth rates slow considerably after sexual maturation. The mass of newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, known as prolarvae, is remarkably low; based on the typical egg diameter of approximately 2.94 millimeters, the wet weight at birth is calculated at 0.0335 grams [Wwb = 0.0335 grams]. This negligible initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva before it must commence exogenous feeding. Following eclosion, the alevin stage is brief, and the larva quickly transitions to an exotrophic, free-swimming existence. The species is typically found in slow-moving, sandy-bottomed stretches of coastal plain streams, where it shelters among leaf litter and submerged debris during daylight hours, emerging at night to forage on benthic invertebrates such as chironomid larvae and small crustaceans.

Sexual maturation in Noturus funebris occurs at a comparatively modest body size. Examination of preserved museum specimens and field-caught individuals has allowed researchers to estimate the total length at puberty at approximately 8 cm [Lp = approximately 8 cm]. This estimate is based on observed gonadal development in related species such as Noturus phaeus, and appears consistent with the onset of vitellogenesis in female Black madtoms. Reaching this developmental threshold typically requires at least one full growing season, after which the fish enters its reproductively viable phase. The transition from immature post-metamorphic juvenile to a sexually mature adult capable of spawning is marked by distinct changes in secondary sexual characteristics, including the development of a more robust head and thickened pectoral spines in males. Breeding individuals are often observed guarding nests in cavities beneath rocks or inside submerged logs, a behavior that underscores the species' investment in parental care. The onset of reproductive activity is tightly linked to seasonal temperature increases and photoperiod cues in its native range.

The maximum reproductive output of this species has been characterized under controlled thermal conditions. In laboratory experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], and reflecting a natural photoperiod, females were observed to produce a maximum clutch size of approximately 27 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 27 eggs per spawning event] combined with a spawning frequency of 4 events per year [F_R_i = 4 events per year], yielding an annual reproductive output of roughly 108 eggs. This annual fecundity represents the maximum rate an individual can sustain given its body size, and it is notably lower than in many larger ictalurids. Each spawning event yields a modest clutch of adhesive demersal eggs, which are deposited in a single layer and vigorously guarded by the male parent until hatching. The reproductive strategy thus appears to emphasize offspring survival through intensive parental care rather than high fecundity. Field observations suggest that not all mature females spawn every year, and that reproductive effort may be constrained by food availability and prior energy reserves accumulated during the active foraging season.

The ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult body mass, of Black madtom has been derived from length-weight regressions based on extensive field sampling. The maximum recorded body mass in adults reaches 25.4 grams [Wwi = 25.4 grams], a value that corresponds closely to individuals approaching the species' maximum total length. This modest mass reflects the elongated, slender body plan typical of benthic-dwelling madtoms, which is adapted for maneuvering within interstitial spaces in the substrate. Body condition varies considerably across the species' range, with individuals in nutrient-rich coastal plain streams often attaining higher weights at equivalent lengths compared to those in more oligotrophic headwater systems. The relationship between length and weight follows a typical allometric pattern, and the derived asymptotic mass provides a useful benchmark for comparing life-history strategies across related Noturus species. Seasonal variation in body mass is also pronounced, with gravid females carrying additional mass from developing oocytes and all individuals accumulating lipid reserves during late summer and autumn to survive the winter period of reduced foraging activity.

Lifespan data for Noturus funebris indicate that this species is relatively short-lived compared to many larger catfishes. The maximum longevity, documented from both mark-recapture studies and captive observations conducted at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], is approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years]. This maximum lifespan in the wild is likely constrained by predation from larger piscivorous fishes and wading birds, as well as by the energetic demands of reproduction. Senescence becomes apparent in the fourth year, with older individuals showing reduced growth increments and a decline in body condition. The oldest documented individuals rarely exceed this age threshold, and post-reproductive survival is minimal. When maintained under stable, predator-free laboratory conditions at 18 °C, individuals occasionally persist for slightly longer than their wild counterparts, though the intrinsic physiological lifespan appears to be hard-limited near the five-year mark.
